title: Single Number
problemStatement: Given a non-empty array of integers nums where every element appears exactly twice except for one which appears exactly once, find that single element. You must implement a solution with O(1) extra space.
approachSteps: Counting occurrences in a hash map would work but costs O(n) space — the O(1)-space requirement is a strong hint to look for a bitwise trick instead.
Recall XOR's key properties: x ^ x = 0 (a number cancels itself out) and x ^ 0 = x, and XOR is commutative/associative (order doesn't matter).
If you XOR every number in the array together, every number that appears exactly twice cancels itself out to 0, leaving only the number that appears once.
So the whole algorithm is: XOR-reduce the entire array into a single accumulator, starting from 0.

bruteForce.approach: Hash map counting occurrences of each number, then scan for the one with count 1.

optimalApproach: XOR every element together; pairs cancel to 0, leaving exactly the single non-paired number.
timeComplexity: O(n) — one pass through the array.
followUps: How would you solve this if every OTHER number appeared exactly THREE times instead of twice (Single Number II)?
How would you find two numbers that each appear once (everything else appears twice) — Single Number III?

title: Counting Bits
problemStatement: Given an integer n, return an array ans of length n+1 where ans[i] is the number of 1's in the binary representation of i, for every i from 0 to n.
approachSteps: Computing each number's bit count independently (e.g. Brian Kernighan's bit trick per number) works but redoes related work — look for a relationship between a number's bit count and a SMALLER, already-computed number's bit count.
Key relationship: for any i, i with its lowest set bit removed is i & (i - 1) — and that operation removes EXACTLY one 1-bit.
So bits(i) = bits(i & (i - 1)) + 1 — the bit count of i is one more than the bit count of a strictly smaller number you've already computed.
Build the answer array bottom-up from 0 to n using that recurrence, since i & (i-1) is always strictly less than i (for i > 0).

bruteForce.approach: For each number from 0 to n, count its bits individually (e.g. right-shift and check the low bit, or Brian Kernighan's n &= n-1 loop).
bruteForce.timeComplexity: O(n log n) — counting bits of each number individually costs O(log value) per number

optimalApproach: DP using the relationship bits(i) = bits(i & (i-1)) + 1, reusing previously computed results instead of recounting bits from scratch for each number.
timeComplexity: O(n) — each of the n+1 entries computed in O(1) using a previously computed result.
spaceComplexity: O(n) for the output array (no extra space beyond that).
followUps: What's an alternative O(n) recurrence using ans[i] = ans[i >> 1] + (i & 1) — why does that also work?
Why does the naive per-number bit-counting approach cost O(log value) per number instead of O(1)?

title: Sum of Two Integers (Without + or -)
problemStatement: Given two integers a and b, return the sum of the two integers without using the + or - operators.
approachSteps: Think about how addition works at the hardware/bit level: for each bit position, you add two bits plus any incoming carry, producing a result bit and an outgoing carry — that's exactly what a hardware adder does, and it's replicable with pure bitwise ops.
XOR (a ^ b) gives the sum of each bit position WITHOUT considering carry — it's correct wherever there's no carry to propagate.
AND (a & b) identifies exactly the bit positions where a carry is generated; shifting that left by 1 ((a & b) << 1) gives where that carry needs to be added in.

So the true sum is (a ^ b) combined with the carry (a & b) << 1 — but combining them also might produce a new carry, so repeat the same XOR/AND process between the running sum and the carry until the carry becomes 0.

In Python specifically, integers have unbounded size (no fixed-width wraparound like in Java/C++), so extra bit-masking is needed to simulate 32-bit two's-complement overflow correctly for negative numbers.

bruteForce.approach: There is no simpler 'brute force' — this is inherently a bit-manipulation problem since +/- are disallowed by the constraints, not just an optimization target.
bruteForce.timeComplexity: N/A — the constraint forces a bitwise approach

optimalApproach: Simulate binary addition: XOR gives the carry-less sum, AND-then-shift gives the carry, and you repeat combining sum and carry (using the same XOR/AND trick) until there's no carry left.
solutionCode:
def get_sum(a, b):
    mask = 0xFFFFFFFF  # simulate 32-bit width
    while b & mask:
        carry = (a & b) << 1
        a = (a ^ b) & mask
        b = carry & mask
    return a if a <= 0x7FFFFFFF else ~(a ^ mask)  # convert back from 32-bit unsigned to signed
timeComplexity: O(1) — at most 32 iterations (bounded by the fixed bit width), independent of the input values' magnitude.
spaceComplexity: O(1) — only a few integer variables.
followUps: Walk through why the final line converts a back to a signed value — what would go wrong without it for negative results?
How would you implement subtraction using this same building block (hint: a - b = a + (-b), and negation can also be done bitwise)?
